nodes.title: The vulnerability occurs when parsing PNG files, which may contain embedded references to other files. A malicious actor could craft a PNG or use an existing one and add a textual chunk type (e.g., tEXt) with the keyword "profile" that ImageMagick interprets as a filename and loads the content as a raw profile. Exploitation path involves crafting a malicious PNG file with a tEXt chunk containing a profile attribute referencing a local file. When ImageMagick is used to process the image, the contents of the referenced files are embedded into the new image. A Proof of Concept (PoC) was tested using a simple Rust application from a GitHub repository. The PoC creates the malicious PNG. The PoC was used to embed the contents of the /etc/passwd file into a PNG image, exploiting CVE-2022-44268. The hex-encoded contents of the /etc/passwd file were successfully embedded inside the PNG as part of the exploit

A malicious actor could craft a PNG or use an existing one and add a textual chunk type (e.g., tEXt) with the keyword "profile" that ImageMagick interprets as a filename and loads the content as a raw profile. Overview of RBCD: RBCD is a s…
nodes.title: Overview of RBCD: RBCD is a security feature in Active Directory introduced with Windows Server 2012; It allows a resource (computer object) to specify which users or machines can impersonate accounts to access its resources; Designed for granular control, it can lead to privilege escalation if misconfigured; Configuration Details: RBCD is configured by modifying the `msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity` attribute on the target resource; This attribute determines which security principals can delegate their privileges to a service running on that resource; Privilege Escalation Process: 1. An attacker gains control over an account (A) that can modify the `msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity` attribute of a target object (B); 2. Using account (A), the attacker requests a Kerberos Service for User to Self (S4U2Self) ticket to impersonate a privileged account; 3. The attacker then requests a Service for User to Proxy (S4U2Proxy) ticket to authenticate services on target machine (B) as the impersonated user; 4. The service ticket obtained can be used with "Pass-the-Ticket" techniques to access the target service as the impersonated user; Exploiting RBCD without Machine Accounts: SPN-less RBCD with User-to-User (U2U) Authentication: Allows RBCD abuse without needing a Service Principal Name (SPN) and even when `MachineAccountQuota` is set to 0; Process includes obtaining a Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) for the SPN-less user, manipulating the password hash, and using S4U2Self and U2U to obtain service tickets; Relaying NTLM Authentication to LDAP: Low-privilege user authentication can be relayed to the Active Directory LDAP service if LDAP signing is not enforced; This allows modification of the `msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity` attribute, setting up RBCD for an attacker-controlled account; Key Requirements for RBCD Attacks: Control over an account that can modify the `msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity` attribute; For classical RBCD, `msDS-MachineAccountQuota` must be greater than 0; For SPN-less RBCD, manipulation of user account properties and U2U Kerberos extension is crucial; In NTLM relaying scenarios, LDAP signing and LDAPS channel binding should not be enforced; Tools for RBCD Exploitation: Impacket: Includes the `getST` script for S4U2Self and S4U2Proxy operations; Rubeus: A C# toolkit for ticket manipulation; Powerview (PowerShell): For enumeration and modifying attributes; Bloody AD: For Active Directory attacks; Ldap_shell: For LDAP interactions; Metasploit: Contains modules for various AD attacks; Next Steps: Risk Assessment: Evaluate the current Active Directory configuration for potential RBCD vulnerabilities and misconfigurations; Mitigation Strategies: Recommend implementing stricter access controls and monitoring for accounts with the ability to modify delegation attributes; Consider enforcing LDAP signing and channel binding to protect against NTLM relaying; Documentation and Reporting: Prepare a detailed report on the RBCD vulnerabilities identified, the potential attack vectors, and recommended remediation steps to enhance the security posture of the Active Directory environment.

nodes.title: Overview of RBCD: RBCD is a security feature in Active Directory introduced with Windows Server 2012; It allows a resource (computer object) to specify which users or machines can impersonate accounts to access its resources; Designed for granular control, it can lead to privilege escalation if misconfigured; Configuration Details: RBCD is configured by modifying the `msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity` attribute on the target resource; This attribute determines which security principals can delegate their privileges to a service running on that resource; Privilege Escalation Process: 1. An attacker gains control over an account (A) that can modify the `msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity` attribute of a target object (B); 2. Using account (A), the attacker requests a Kerberos Service for User to Self (S4U2Self) ticket to impersonate a privileged account; 3. The attacker then requests a Service for User to Proxy (S4U2Proxy) ticket to authenticate services on target machine (B) as the impersonated user; 4. The service ticket obtained can be used with "Pass-the-Ticket" techniques to access the target service as the impersonated user; Exploiting RBCD without Machine Accounts: SPN-less RBCD with User-to-User (U2U) Authentication: Allows RBCD abuse without needing a Service Principal Name (SPN) and even when `MachineAccountQuota` is set to 0; Process includes obtaining a Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) for the SPN-less user, manipulating the password hash, and using S4U2Self and U2U to obtain service tickets; Relaying NTLM Authentication to LDAP: Low-privilege user authentication can be relayed to the Active Directory LDAP service if LDAP signing is not enforced; This allows modification of the `msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity` attribute, setting up RBCD for an attacker-controlled account; Key Requirements for RBCD Attacks: Control over an account that can modify the `msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity` attribute; For classical RBCD, `msDS-MachineAccountQuota` must be greater than 0; For SPN-less RBCD, manipulation of user account properties and U2U Kerberos extension is crucial; In NTLM relaying scenarios, LDAP signing and LDAPS channel binding should not be enforced; Tools for RBCD Exploitation: Impacket: Includes the `getST` script for S4U2Self and S4U2Proxy operations; Rubeus: A C# toolkit for ticket manipulation; Powerview (PowerShell): For enumeration and modifying attributes; Bloody AD: For Active Directory attacks; Ldap_shell: For LDAP interactions; Metasploit: Contains modules for various AD attacks; Next Steps: Risk Assessment: Evaluate the current Active Directory configuration for potential RBCD vulnerabilities and misconfigurations; Mitigation Strategies: Recommend implementing stricter access controls and monitoring for accounts with the ability to modify delegation attributes; Consider enforcing LDAP signing and channel binding to protect against NTLM relaying; Documentation and Reporting: Prepare a detailed report on the RBCD vulnerabilities identified, the potential attack vectors, and recommended remediation steps to enhance the security posture of the Active Directory environment.

1. **Check of Previous Step Achievement**: The intended task of the previous steps, particularly the enumeration of the HTTP service on port 80, was achieved successfully. The penetration testing tree shows that information was gathered about the web server, including the presence of a login feature and the need to adjust the hosts file to resolve the virtual host. Additionally, an attempt to use Gobuster for directory brute-forcing led to a temporary ban, indicating that the server has active security measures against automated scanning tools.

2. **Key Findings and Their Implications**: The key findings from the enumeration of port 80's HTTP service include:
   - **Server Hardening**: The server's response to the Gobuster scan with a temporary ban suggests robust monitoring and response mechanisms to scanning attempts, indicating a higher level of security.
   - **Virtual Host Information**: The discovery of a specific virtual host (supersecurehotel.htb) suggests that there may be additional content served under this domain, potentially accessible by adjusting local DNS resolution (hosts file).
   - **Login Feature**: The presence of a login option indicates potentially exploitable authentication mechanisms or session management flaws.

   These findings suggest that while port 80 is hardened against certain types of attacks, it might still contain vulnerabilities, particularly related to its web applications. However, the active security measures complicate further direct scanning or brute-forcing attempts.

3. **Strategy Evaluation and Next Steps**: Given the robust security measures encountered on port 80 and the complications in further scanning without potentially triggering additional security responses, it is logical to shift focus to another entry point. Port 64999, also running an HTTP service, presents itself as a viable alternative target for further exploration. This port may have different security configurations or less stringent monitoring compared to port 80, providing a new avenue for discovering vulnerabilities. The strategy to move to enumerating port 64999 is based on:
   - **Diversification of Attack Surface**: Exploring different services to identify the least secure entry point.
   - **Potential for Lesser Security Measures**: Given that port 80 has shown strong security responses, port 64999 might be configured differently and could potentially offer more fruitful results without immediate banning.

This strategic shift is supported by the principle of attacking the weakest link in the security chain and adapting the attack strategy based on the system's response to initial testing efforts.

The intended task was to uncover hidden directories, links, and software details through manual inspection. This parameter appears to be dynamically influencing the content or database queries, suggesting its use in database interactions. This is a critical observation because:
   - **Potential SQL Injection Vector**: The presence of a query parameter directly influencing database interactions is a classic entry point for SQL injection attacks, where malicious SQL statements could be inserted into the query to manipulate or exploit the database.
   - **Vulnerability Assessment Opportunity**: Since automated scans and other enumeration strategies have not revealed significant vulnerabilities, focusing on potential SQL injection through this parameter offers a new avenue to test the robustness of the application’s input handling and database security settings.

3. **Strategy Evaluation and Next Steps**: Given the discovery of a potentially exploitable query parameter, the strategy to attempt an SQL injection is both logical and warranted. This involves:
   - **Testing for SQL Injection**: Utilizing tools or manual techniques to test how the application handles SQL code inserted into the "cod" parameter. This can help determine if the application is vulnerable to SQL injection, which could allow unauthorized database access or manipulation.
   - **Expanding Attack Surface Understanding**: If an SQL injection vulnerability is found, it could provide deeper access to the application's backend, revealing more about the data structure and potentially uncovering further vulnerabilities.
   - **Ethical and Legal Considerations**: It’s crucial to ensure that all testing is authorized and conducted within the bounds of ethical hacking guidelines to prevent legal issues and ensure the integrity of the target system is not compromised.

This shift in strategy to attempt an SQL injection attack is based on the specific findings from the manual review of the application and represents a focused attempt to uncover high-impact vulnerabilities that automated tools failed to detect. This approach leverages the specific insight gained about the application's functionality and directly tests the security of user input handling, which is a common vulnerability in web applications.

new_strategy: Try to create a reverese shell using the write permissions
strategy_explanation:
1. **Evaluation of Previous Step Achievement**: The prior steps in the penetration testing task list (PTT) focused on exploiting SQL injection vulnerabilities and assessing the server's file interaction capabilities. The results confirmed that:
   - **SQL Injection was Successful**: The ability to inject SQL and retrieve sensitive information such as the database version, current database user, and read system files (`/etc/passwd`) was established.
   - **File Interaction Capabilities**: The server's configuration was inspected, revealing that files could potentially be written to the server using MySQL’s `INTO OUTFILE` function, targeting the configured DocumentRoot. This indicates write permissions that could be exploited.

2. **Key Findings and Implications for Further Steps**:
   - **Write Permissions Confirmed**: The ability to potentially write files to the server's document root is a significant security vulnerability. Given that the server allows for file writing through SQL commands, this can be exploited to upload malicious files, such as a web shell.
   - **Potential for Reverse Shell**: By writing a web shell to the server, an attacker could execute arbitrary commands on the server, potentially escalating to a reverse shell. This would provide the attacker with interactive control over the server, simulating full system access.

3. **Strategy Evaluation and Next Steps**:
   - **Moving Forward with Reverse Shell Creation**: The strategy to use the confirmed write permissions to create a reverse shell is a logical progression from the current findings. This involves:
     - **Writing a Web Shell**: Crafting a SQL query to write a simple PHP web shell into the server’s web directory using the `INTO OUTFILE` SQL command. The web shell would include functions to execute system commands.
     - **Executing the Web Shell for Reverse Shell**: Once the web shell is in place, it can be accessed via a web browser to execute a reverse shell command, which connects back to a listener set up by the tester on their machine.
   - **Ethical and Legal Considerations**: As with all penetration testing activities, this step must be authorized and should aim to identify and report vulnerabilities without causing harm or unauthorized data access.

Given the critical nature of the vulnerabilities identified and the potential for significant system control, moving forward with the strategy to create a reverse shell using the write permissions is both strategically sound and necessary for demonstrating the impact of the vulnerabilities. This step will help in understanding the full extent of potential system compromise and assist in prioritizing security measures to mitigate such risks.

1. **Assessment of Current Strategic Position**: According to the updated PTT, the previous steps confirmed the server's susceptibility to SQL injection and demonstrated the ability to interact with the file system, specifically using the `INTO OUTFILE` SQL command. This indicates that the server permits writing files to a specified directory, which is a significant security vulnerability.

2. **Key Findings Leading to Further Steps**:
   - **Confirmed Write Permissions**: The ability to write files to the server's document root through SQL commands was established. This opens up the possibility of uploading arbitrary files, such as a web shell.
   - **Potential for Reverse Shell**: The presence of write permissions can be exploited to upload a web shell, which can then be used to execute system commands remotely. This could potentially escalate to gaining a reverse shell, providing interactive control over the server.

3. **Logical Progression to Selected Step**:
   - **Writing a Web Shell**: The next logical step is to exploit the write permissions to upload a web shell. This can be achieved by crafting a SQL query that uses the `INTO OUTFILE` command to write a PHP script into the server's web directory. The PHP script would be designed to execute system commands passed to it via HTTP requests.
   - **Gaining Reverse Shell Access**: Once the web shell is successfully uploaded and accessible via the web server, it can be used to initiate a reverse shell. This involves sending a command through the web shell that triggers a connection back to a listener (controlled by the tester) on another machine. This reverse shell would allow for full, interactive control over the server, mimicking the capabilities of an authenticated user.

4. **Ethical and Security Considerations**:
   - **Controlled Testing Environment**: It is crucial to ensure that these actions are conducted in a controlled environment where they are authorized. This step is aimed at demonstrating the potential impact of the vulnerability and helping system administrators understand the need for stringent security measures.
   - **Mitigation and Reporting**: Following the demonstration, it is necessary to report the findings and recommend measures to secure the file writing capabilities and address the SQL injection vulnerabilities, thus preventing potential exploitation by malicious actors.

By moving forward with the strategy to write a web shell and attempt to gain reverse shell access, we are directly building upon the established vulnerabilities to demonstrate a critical security risk. This approach not only tests the server's response to more advanced exploitation techniques but also helps in prioritizing security enhancements to mitigate these vulnerabilities.

new_strategy: Enumerate the files, commands and their privileges to escalate the privilege
strategy_explanation:
1. **Evaluation of Previous Step Achievement**:
   - The previous steps in the penetration testing task list (PTT) successfully exploited SQL injection vulnerabilities to write a web shell (`pwned.php`) onto the server. This allowed for remote command execution which confirmed that commands were executed with the web server user privileges (`www-data`).
   - A reverse shell was also successfully established, providing interactive access to the server as the `www-data` user.

2. **Key Findings and Implications for Further Steps**:
   - **Access as `www-data`**: The current level of access is under the `www-data` user, which typically has limited privileges on the server. This user is used primarily for running the web server and has restricted access to critical system files and processes.
   - **Potential for Privilege Escalation**: Given the limited privileges of the `www-data` user, escalating privileges is essential for deeper system access. Privilege escalation can expose more sensitive areas of the system, potentially leading to administrative access.

3. **Strategy Evaluation and Next Steps**:
   - **Enumerate Files, Commands, and Privileges**: The next logical step is to enumerate the server for misconfigurations, vulnerable software versions, or writable configuration files that could be exploited to escalate privileges. This involves:
     - **Checking Sudo Rights**: Enumerate which commands can be run with sudo, particularly looking for misconfigurations that allow executing commands as a superuser without a password.
     - **Version and Patch Level Checking**: Identify the versions of the operating system and installed software to check against known vulnerabilities that might be exploited for privilege escalation.
     - **Writable Directories and Files**: Look for directories and files with improper permissions that might allow modifying scripts or binaries used by higher-privileged users.
   - **Continuation of Current Strategy**: Moving forward with privilege escalation is a direct continuation of the established access. It builds upon the current foothold to potentially gain full control over the system, which is the ultimate goal of penetration testing to identify and mitigate security risks.

Given the successful establishment of a reverse shell and the limited privileges associated with the `www-data` user, the strategy to enumerate files, commands, and their privileges to escalate privileges is both necessary and logical. This step will help in identifying further security weaknesses and enhancing the security posture of the system by addressing these escalation vectors.
gold_new_step: Explore the suspicious files, commands and create a summary of the findings.
gold_step_explanation:
1. **Assessment of Current Strategic Position**:
   - The updated PTT indicates that we have successfully established a reverse shell with `www-data` user privileges on the target system. This level of access serves as a foundational step towards deeper system exploration and potential privilege escalation.
   - The aim now is to leverage the existing access to explore further vulnerabilities or misconfigurations that could allow for higher-level privileges.

2. **Key Findings Leading to Further Steps**:
   - **Limited Privileges of `www-data`**: The `www-data` user typically has restricted access, which limits the ability to view or alter critical system files directly. However, this user can often access various logs, temporary files, and some configuration files, which can be scrutinized for sensitive information or misconfigurations.
   - **Potential for Privilege Escalation**: Given the nature of the `www-data` user, the system may contain other vulnerabilities or misconfigurations in files or commands that the `www-data` user can access. These can potentially be exploited to escalate privileges.

3. **Logical Progression to Selected Step**:
   - **Exploring Suspicious Files and Commands**: The strategy involves methodically searching through the file system, particularly focusing on:
     - **Config Files and Scripts**: Many applications and system services store configurations in files that might have insecure permissions or contain credentials.
     - **Scheduled Tasks and Cron Jobs**: These might be configured to run scripts or commands as a higher-privileged user. Modifying these scripts or exploiting path vulnerabilities could lead to privilege escalation.
     - **Version and Patch Information**: Software with known vulnerabilities (which can be identified through version numbers) may allow exploitation if patches or updates have not been applied.
   - **Creating a Summary of Findings**: Documenting each potential vulnerability or misconfiguration found during the enumeration process. This summary will not only aid in understanding the current security posture but also guide the exploitation phase to escalate privileges effectively.

4. **Ethical and Security Considerations**:
   - **Controlled Exploration**: Ensure that the exploration is tightly scoped to avoid unnecessary system changes or disruptions. This step should be purely diagnostic and non-destructive.
   - **Documentation and Reporting**: Accurately documenting findings is crucial for remediation efforts. The summary should be detailed, pointing out specific misconfigurations, vulnerable software, or insecure permissions that could be addressed to enhance system security.

By moving forward with the strategy to explore suspicious files, commands, and their privileges, we are building upon the initial access to uncover deeper vulnerabilities. This approach is essential for a thorough security assessment, aiming to identify all possible vectors for privilege escalation and ultimately securing the system against such exploits.

   - The previous steps in the penetration testing task list (PTT) successfully exploited a command injection vulnerability in the `simpler.py` script, allowing the execution of arbitrary commands as the user `pepper` via a reverse shell. This was confirmed by the successful execution of a reverse shell script that connected back to the attacker's machine, providing shell access as `pepper`.
   - This accomplishment is significant as it marks the transition from the lower-privileged `www-data` user to the `pepper` user, potentially opening up new avenues for further exploration and exploitation within the system.

2. **Key Findings and Implications for Further Steps**:
   - **Achieved User Privilege Level**: Gaining access as the `pepper` user suggests that there may be additional sensitive files, commands, or services accessible that were not available to `www-data`. This user might have different permissions or access controls set, which could lead to further privilege escalation opportunities.
   - **Potential for Further Privilege Escalation**: Given that `pepper` is likely to have different and potentially more extensive privileges than `www-data`, there is a strong rationale to investigate this user’s environment more thoroughly. This includes checking for sudo privileges, cron jobs, writable configuration files, or other executables that `pepper` can run with elevated privileges.

3. **Strategy Evaluation and Next Steps**:
   - **Enumerate the Machine**: The next logical step is to conduct a thorough enumeration of the machine from the perspective of the `pepper` user. This includes listing directory contents, checking running processes, reviewing scheduled tasks, and examining user permissions and group memberships.
   - **Identify Privilege Escalation Vectors**: During enumeration, special attention should be given to finding misconfigurations, unprotected files or scripts that `pepper` can edit, and commands or applications that `pepper` can execute with sudo privileges without a password. Tools like `linpeas` or manual checks such as `sudo -l`, checking `/etc/cron*` directories, and `.bash_history` can be invaluable here.
   - **Continue with the Current Strategy**: Since gaining access as `pepper` has opened up new potential for discovering vulnerabilities, continuing with the strategy of enumerating the system for further privilege escalation paths is both necessary and promising. This step is crucial for a deeper penetration into the system, aiming to gain root access or access to sensitive data.

Given the successful elevation to the `pepper` user and the potential for uncovering new vulnerabilities or misconfigurations at this higher privilege level, the strategy to enumerate the system is well-founded and essential. new_strategy: Find a method to use systemctl link command to escalate privileges
strategy_explanation:
1. **Evaluation of Previous Step Achievement**:
   - The previous step in the penetration testing task list (PTT) was focused on enumerating SUID files on the system. This step was successfully completed, and key findings were documented. Among the SUID files found, `systemctl` was identified as having SUID permissions, which is unusual because `systemctl` typically does not have SUID permissions by default.
   - This finding is significant as it indicates a potential misconfiguration that could be exploited for privilege escalation, given the capabilities of `systemctl` in managing system services.

2. **Key Findings and Implications for Further Steps**:
   - **Unusual SUID Permission on Systemctl**: The presence of SUID permissions on `systemctl` suggests that it can be run with root privileges by any user. This is a critical finding because `systemctl` can control services, potentially allowing an attacker to manipulate these services to execute arbitrary code as the root user.
   - **Potential Exploitation Path**: The ability to use `systemctl` to link and manage custom or malicious service files could lead to a privilege escalation. This method involves creating a new service file that executes a chosen command or script with root privileges and then using `systemctl` to enable and start this service.

3. **Strategy Evaluation and Next Steps**:
   - **Exploitation of Systemctl SUID Configuration**: Given the current findings, the next logical step is to exploit the SUID configuration of `systemctl`. This involves crafting a malicious service file that, when executed as a service, will run with root privileges, effectively escalating the privileges of the attacker from a lower-privileged user to root.
   - **Methodology for Privilege Escalation**:
     - Create a malicious service file that includes a command to execute a reverse shell or a similar payload.
     - Use the `systemctl link` command to add this service to the system's service management.
     - Start the service using `systemctl start`, which will execute the payload with root privileges due to the SUID bit set on `systemctl`.
   - **Continue with the Current Strategy**: The discovery of the SUID bit set on `systemctl` provides a clear pathway for privilege escalation. It is both necessary and promising to continue with this strategy as it directly leverages the identified misconfiguration for security testing.

The strategy to exploit the SUID configuration of `systemctl` is well-founded based on the security implications of the findings. This approach is crucial for demonstrating the potential security risk associated with misconfigurations and for providing concrete examples of how such vulnerabilities could be exploited in real-world scenarios. This step is essential for enhancing the overall security posture of the system by addressing and mitigating discovered vulnerabilities.

nodes.title:
1.3.4 Vulnerability Analysis on Dolibarr 12.0.3 [unknown]
Vulnerability Identifier: CVE-2020-35136, Type: Authenticated Remote Code Execution (RCE), Date Identified: December 23, 2020, Description: The vulnerability arises from improper neutralization of special elements in commands within the backup function of Dolibarr 12.0.3. An authenticated attacker with access to the administrator dashboard can exploit this by manipulating the `zipfilename_template` parameter in `admin/tools/dolibarr_export.php`. Impact: Successful exploitation can lead to complete system compromise, allowing arbitrary code execution with web server privileges. CVSS Scores: CVSS v3.1 Base Score: 7.2 (HIGH), CVSS v2.0 Base Score: 9.0 (HIGH). Technical Details: The issue is due to a lack of proper sanitization of the `zipfilename_template` parameter, enabling command injection through crafted filenames. Mitigation and Remediation: A patch has been released that restricts the use of the `--` string in filenames. Organizations using Dolibarr 12.0.3 are strongly advised to upgrade to a patched version. Fix implemented via commit: `4fcd3fe49332baab0e424225ad10b76b47ebcbac`. Further References: NVD - CVE-2020-35136: [NVD Link](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2020-35136), GitHub Advisory: [GitHub Link](https://github.com/doli/dolibarr/security/advisories/GHSA-7gq7-hjgr-83g9), Wiz Blog on CVE-2020-35136: [Wiz Link](https://www.wiz.io/blog/cve-2020-35136-impact-exploitability-and-mitigation-steps), Exploit-DB Entry: [Exploit-DB Link](https://www.exploit-db.com/exploits/49269).

new_strategy: Add a computer account the active directory
strategy_explanation:
1. The intended task of the previous step was to explore the Active Directory and analyze the certificates. This task was successfully achieved using the tool certipy v4.8.2. 

2. The key findings from this step are that it found 37 certificate templates and 1 certificate authority. Among these, 13 certificate templates were enabled. A specific template named 'CorpVPN' was found to be enabled and allows client authentication. A vulnerability was found: 'AUTHORITY.HTB\\Domain Computers' can enroll, the enrollee supplies the subject, and the template allows client authentication. 

3. Given these findings, it is clear that there is a potential vulnerability in the 'CorpVPN' certificate template. The fact that all domain computers can enroll and the enrollee supplies the subject, indicates that there is potential for abuse. This is known as the ESC1 vulnerability. The logical next step is to add a computer account to the Active Directory. By adding a computer account, we can enroll it for a certificate using the 'CorpVPN' template and potentially exploit the ESC1 vulnerability to escalate our privileges or gain further access to the system. Therefore, it makes sense to move forward with this strategy.
gold_new_step: Exploit the selected exploitations
gold_step_explanation:
1. The selected step is to exploit the identified vulnerabilities, specifically the ESC1 vulnerability in the 'CorpVPN' certificate template.

2. The chain-of-thoughts leading to this step begins with the successful exploration of the Active Directory and analysis of certificates. This exploration revealed a vulnerability in the 'CorpVPN' certificate template, which allows all domain computers to enroll and the enrollee supplies the subject. 

3. The next link in the chain is the strategy to add a computer account to the Active Directory. Adding a computer account provides an opportunity to enroll it for a certificate using the 'CorpVPN' template. 

4. The final link in the chain is the exploitation of the identified vulnerability. Here, the aim is to add a new user to the Active Directory and request a certificate specifying the built-in domain Administrator account as the Subject Alternative Name (SAN). The SAN is an extension to X.509 that allows various values to be associated with a security certificate. In this case, associating the new user with the domain Administrator account could potentially allow us to escalate our privileges or gain further access to the system.

5. Therefore, the logical step is to exploit the identified vulnerability by adding a new user to the Active Directory, requesting a certificate for this user, and specifying the built-in domain Administrator account as the SAN. This could potentially allow us to escalate our privileges or gain further access to the system.
